Swirl continuation · a shipping law for all 64 sizes at k = −1

Two dials between every exact swirl

A swirl's continuation is fixed by a palindrome of gap equations, and a palindrome leaves two of its unknowns free. So a size is never unsolvable — it has a whole family of exact answers, and picking one is arithmetic, not search. The two free parameters are the dials below: the gap every lace lands on, and the floor the corners are held to. Both hands, all 64 sizes, every gap on its target to 10⁻¹² px — checked here by the aligner's own test, live, at whatever setting you leave the dials on. What the dials cost is corner clearance and arm length, and the page shows you both.

Both plates are the same stitch: the woven starting block, its masks, then the two continuation groups laid over it, exactly the order the reference sheet draws in. The left plate is the configuration stored in the file for this size and hand; the right is the one the law derives from m, n and the two dials — nothing here is a picture, and nothing here is searched. Dashed rules are the gaps, measured between consecutive extended starts, and the ring is the tightest corner with its signed margin. The plate keeps one paper in both themes because these are the sheet's own strand colours.

Why two dials and not one number

The family was always there

A continuation group of p pairs puts 2p arms on the block, and the pair index reads 0, 1, …, p−1, p−1, …, 1, 0. Because that order is a palindrome the interior gap equations come in identical pairs, so of the 2p−1 equations only p are distinct — against p+2 unknowns, the p extensions plus the shared angle and the gap itself. Two unknowns are left over. That is not slack in the model; it is the shape of the problem.

Fix the gap g and the angle θ and every extension telescopes out of the middle pair, one subtraction at a time, in closed form. So the whole family is reachable by choosing two numbers — and the file's stored configurations, hand-steered or solver-picked size by size, are all members of it.

The aligner never saw the family. It searches a ±20° window around each arm's unextended direction and ranks what it finds by least extension, which is the member sitting on the edge of the feasible cone — the one where the shallowest arm empties to exactly zero. That is a fine member and it is the one this law takes for a multi-pair group. But at the one-pair boundary it is the member the corner check rejects, and the window is narrow enough to cut real answers off entirely: at the canonical gap the derived angle for 1 × 8 sits 2.3° outside it, and 1 × 7 0.8° outside.

So the boundary takes the corner as an input. Instead of solving the one-pair group and checking the corner afterwards, the law computes the uncorrected margin M₀ from the transposed group and extends by exactly what carries it to M★. The floor is then never approached — it is hit, to the last decimal, at every size on the boundary.

Q = 8 + 112m R = 24 − 112m U = (g − 56 cos θ)/sin θ − Q V = −(g + 168 cos θ)/sin θ − Q ep−1 = Tp−1/2 ej = Tj − ej+1 Tj = U for odd j, V for even j e0 = (R sin θ − 144 cos θ − sin θ·e1 − g)/cos θ cone edge A cos θ + B sin θ = C, A = 56a + 168b, B = Q(a+b), C = (a−b)g boundary M₀ = 88 sin φ + (32+p₀) cos φ, E = max(0, (M★ − M₀)/sin φ)

The coefficients a and b record how much of U and V the shallow pair r = min(2, p−1) carries; they come off a two-line recurrence walking outward from the centre pair. 1 × 1 is its own exact 45° case, g = √2(32 + E).

What the dials cost

Every setting is exact; not every setting is safe

The gap dial is the expensive one, and it is expensive twice over. Opening it pushes each group's outside pair further across the other group's starting corners — the tightest corner anywhere is +16.00 px on the floor at 56, +7.45 by 58, and crosses zero at 58.96 — and it lengthens every arm to reach the wider spacing, which runs into the aligner's own 200 px cap sooner, at 57.41. That is the widest gap the whole family survives, and it is what the second button sets. Past 66 px some sizes leave the feasible cone altogether and there is no exact member left to pick at all.

The corner-floor dial is the cheap one, and it saturates. Only the one-pair boundary spends it, so raising it lengthens fifteen sizes' outer arms and touches nothing else — and past about 16.6 px the multi-pair interior is the tightest thing in the family anyway, so more floor buys arm length and no more clearance.

Shipping it

What changes in the generator

  1. Derive the configuration instead of searching for it

    The aligner's job becomes evaluating F(m, n) at the two dial values and returning it. The ±20° window and the ranking pass go away with it — they are what made 1 × 7 and 1 × 8 look unsolvable, and they cannot rank a member they never generate.

    the aligner · the angle window and the least-extension ranking

  2. Give the whole stitch one gap, not one per group

    Ten of the sixty-four stored sizes run their two groups on different gaps — 1 × 4 through 1 × 8 and their transposes, sitting around 56 across and 58–62 down. The law takes g once and both groups land on it, so the target is a single constant and the split disappears.

    the stored preset table · the two per-group gap fields

  3. Make the corner floor an input to the boundary case

    M★ stops being a threshold the corner check compares against and becomes the number Case C extends to reach. The check then only ever confirms what was constructed, which is the whole point: the floor is hit exactly rather than cleared by luck.

    the corner measurement · the n = 1 and m = 1 boundary

  4. Re-record the 128 handed entries as a derived table

    Every entry becomes (m, n, hand, g, M★) and the geometry follows. Keep the hand-steered configurations that differ — 3 × 1 at E = 15.1646 for a +16.22 corner against the law's E = 14.8117 for +16.0000 — as named alternates, since they are the same family, chosen by eye.

    the stored presets · both hands, 1 × 1 through 8 × 8

  5. Turn the gap test into an assertion

    At any dial setting inside the safe range the gap equations are satisfied outright, so the test can stop reporting a score and start refusing to build: assert every gap equals g and name the arm that fails. That is what keeps the law honest once the search is gone.

    the aligner's gap test · the 64-size replay

Every number on this page is computed in the page. The construction is the piecewise function F(m, n) — Case A for 1 × 1, Case B for a multi-pair group, Case C for the one-pair boundary — and it is scored by the aligner's own gap test and corner measurement, re-implemented here line for line and run against the generator's own geometry for all 128 handed entries. At the canonical setting (g = 56.01 px, M★ = 16 px) it reproduces the published Case C table to 5 × 10⁻⁷ °, puts every gap on target to 6 × 10⁻¹³ px, and holds every corner at or above +16.0000 px: Case A alone at +39.60, the multi-pair interior +16.63 … +32.94, the boundary +16.0000 across the board. 1 × 1 has no k = −1 in range and is drawn at the one twist it has.
